title: Liturgy
description: What is done, and in what order.
html:
Read in the Ide dialect. The original is written in Igbo; here the one term that changes is chi → si, Ide has chi: it is the word, and si / sị is how it is widely said. Nothing here is rewritten — the documents stand as written.

IN THIS DOCUMENT

Contents

5. The declaration:

The liturgy of Odiana

What is said and done: the daily office, the offering, the rites of life, the cleansing, the year.

No blood is brought to a shrine or an altar anywhere in this liturgy, and nothing in it is blooded. Where the rite is a festival or a serious rite of the religion, an animal is killed — in the open, beyond the shrine. Where the rite is an inherited one, the words in quotation marks are the sources'; where the sources give a form and no words, the words are composed and are marked composed.

1 · The daily office

The floor of the religion, and the tradition's own specification:

kola and water in a small round wooden bowl — before the household altar, at the chi's place.

The full form adds palm wine and a small food. "In all worships, offerings consist mostly of kola nut and palm oil."

| hour | what is done | |---|---| | dawn | face east, and take the early sun — "the best form of spiritual hygiene and the greatest instrument for conducting morning rituals". Then sweep the ground with a palm broom, and take the sweepings away | | then | wash at the threshold, and make the offering | | dusk | the offering again, the water vessels emptied and refilled, and the ground walked once |

And the kola is served in an order, because the order is the doctrine: "genealogical distance, the social distance, social differentiation; and of course, status structure." Where the gathered are not one another's kin — which is most of the time in a temple — the tradition's own rule is that "an expanded 'model' is invented to accommodate the new situation", and the priest states the order aloud before serving.

2 · The seven steps

The sources' only ordered bloodless rite, and the spine of everything else here. Inherited in form; the words are composed.

| # | step | what is done | |---|---|---| | 1 | Isa aka | wash the hands | | 2 | Itu nzu | take up nzu as "a point of contact" | | 3 | Ikpoku mmụọ | call the chi, the four market days, and the ancestors | | 4 | introducing yourself | name · the market day you were born · your parents · your town. A registered identity — recorded at the Ndose | | 5 | Itu mmanya | libation | | 6 | Iweta oji — kola, or the ofo | and if you have neither, the rite continues: "it is still okay to make your declarations using your nzu or whatever you have present" | | 7 | Isee | the rite is sealed |

Step six's substitution clause is kept — the tradition licensing its own economy. A religion that requires a particular object for prayer has priced out the poor, and Odiana will not.

The words, composed

The priest: "Ana, hear. Chi m, greet me."

The people: Isee — it is so.

The priest: "Anyị bụ mkpụrụ unu; unu bụ mgbọrọgwụ anyị." — We are your seeds; you are our roots.

The people: Isee.

The priest: "Ụzọ anyị dị ọcha; aka anyị dị ọcha; anyị abịaghị iwere ihe n'ike." — Our way is clean;

our hands are clean; we have not come to take anything by force.

The people: Isee.

3 · The offering — nchu aja

Odiana performs nchu aja to the high God, and performs it bloodless — because the offering to Chukwu was always bloodless, and because no blood is ever brought to the altar of this religion (canon.md A1–A4, A6, A11). The animal of a festival or a serious rite is a different matter, and it is killed in the open.

What is laid: oji (kola) · water in a small round wooden bowl · mmanya (palm wine) · nzu · the first fruits · a small food · white cloth · and the words.

What is not: anything living, anything killed, anything whose taking caused suffering, and anything that would foul the ground or the water. The rule of the temple is the rule of the religion: nothing used pollutes land or water.

And the offering is made pointing the kola at the sun — which is how the tradition offers to the supreme being, reaching the highest tier by gesture, not by blood.

4 · Birth

Inherited in substance.

The family presents the newborn to the priest of their Ndose, who blesses the child and welcomes them into the community of the living. The parents announce the child's sacred name — the name given in connection with the child's own chi — together with the family and personal names, spoken aloud before witnesses. Kola, fruit or another wholesome food is shared. No blood, no bodily substance, and nothing is placed in the newborn's mouth. The birth is recorded by the Ndose.

The blessing:

"Aha gị bụ ndụ gị; chi gị bụrụ ụzọ gị; Ana gị bụrụ be gị; Chukwu nyekwuo gị ume."

Your name is your life; may your chi be your path; may Ana be your home; God give you strength.

Then the cord is buried — "preferably at the foot of an economic tree, which for most areas, is the oil palm tree" — with an economic plant or a symbolic gift, and no animal. That rite confers standing in the community, and it is bloodless: "the status of a freeborn is symbolized by the burial of his navel cord."

And the first water. The child's first pot of water is presented "to the most senior woman" of the family — the officiant is female by rule, so the women's order has its own rite at the very start of life.

5 · Marriage — Igba nkwu

Inherited in substance.

Marriage is the joining of two people, their families and their communities — not the purchase or transfer of a woman, but a covenant freely entered by two adults.

1. The couple chooses the priest of the Ndose whose authority they wish over the marriage. He officiates, with the families and the community as witnesses. 2. The groom and his family bring a gift of fellowship — food, cloth, livestock, craft, or whatever is within their means. It has no fixed value, is not payment for the bride, and can never be demanded as a condition of marriage. 3. The bride takes a cup of palm wine and walks among the gathered to the man she has chosen, and presents it. He must receive it and drink from it — he may not pour it away, for drinking is his public declaration that he accepts her choice and enters the covenant willingly. 4. The priest joins their hands, prays to chi, Ana and the ancestors, and asks both to affirm their consent.

5. The declaration:

"Unu abụrụla otu ụzọ; ka ụzọ unu bụrụ nke udo."

You have become one path; may your path be one of peace.

No woman is bought, and no family sells a daughter.

6 · Burial

Inherited in substance; bloodless throughout.

The priest of the deceased's Ndose leads the rites; the family and the lineage fulfil their parts.

1 · Preparation. The body is washed with clean water and dressed in white cloth. No embalming and no chemical preservation. A relic is taken before the casket is sealed — the tradition's own practice — and is prepared for the lineage's keeping. No grave is reopened for this purpose.

2 · The casket. Woven fibre only, and biodegradable — metal, plastic, cement, chemical treatments and embalming are forbidden. Flowers are honour and remembrance and carry no ritual function.

3 · The blessing of return:

"Ihe Ana nyere, Ana na-anata. Ka ahụ laghachi n'Ana, ka chi gị gaa n'ụzọ ya."

What Ana gives, Ana receives. May the body return to Ana, and may your chi continue upon its path.

4 · The return. Burial is always in the ground, and the grave faces east. The grave adapts to dry land, wetland or mangrove, but the casket is never placed in standing water. Families may plant herbs above it as living memorials.

5 · Continuity. The relic goes to the lineage's keeping, worked into the designated artefact. The grave itself remains undisturbed.

7 · Confession — Nchegharị

A person carrying guilt may seek the keeper of confession. The meeting is secret, held away from the Ndose and the community, and the keeper is bound to silence. The person confesses truthfully, without fear of public shame.

Confession does not erase consequences. Where another person has been harmed, the keeper may require restitution, reconciliation, service or another act appropriate to the wrong — and where restitution would endanger the innocent or expose a victim to further harm, he must seek a safer path.

"Ana anụla gị. I kwuola eziokwu. Gbanwee obi gị, dozie ihe ị mebiri, jee n'udo."

Ana has heard you. You have spoken the truth. Change your heart, repair what you have damaged, and go in

peace.

No priest may use what is confessed for advantage, humiliation, revenge or gossip. "For Nchegharị is not the hiding of wrongdoing; it is the beginning of making right what has been made wrong."

And the titled body confesses publicly. The Ozo order keeps an annual public confession, in which a titled man declares his wrongs before the community — "enforced by belief that concealment brings immediate illness followed by a disgraceful death." That is the moral engine of the order, and Odiana keeps it.

8 · Cleansing and consecration

The ordinary cleansing, in seven steps — for a person or a place, performed by a licensed priest:

| # | what is done | |---|---| | 1 | the ground is cleared, and the boundary re-marked with nzu | | 2 | water is poured — at the threshold and at the altar | | 3 | the surfaces are washed with water infused with nzu | | 4 | ogilisi or uziza is burned, and the smoke carried through the space | | 5 | white cloth is laid or hung | | 6 | the declaration, by the priest, answered by those present | | 7 | the water is taken away, and poured where it will not foul anything |

The greater cleansing, for an alu, is the same seven steps with the community present, the restitution the law requires, and a period of keeping the daily discipline without exception. There is no bloodless substitute for a major ikpu alu in the sources, and this is an innovation (canon.md A5).

Consecrating an Ndose, in six parts — white cloth · clean water on the altar and emblems · nzu · kola · the prayer · libation. No object is consecrated with blood (A6).

9 · Ordination, and the taking of titles

The priesthood

The priesthood is not hereditary and it is a vocation — "the priesthood is not an acquired title but a vocation", and the candidate is "sought", not self-appointed.

And the rule that orders it: "Every minor-spirit priest must receive his ofo from the earth-priest." So no priest officiates without ofo received through the eze ana — authority descends from the earth priest, not from a committee.

The ordination is bloodless, in three parts:

1. the candidate's standing is established by the cord-burial rite — the tradition's own bloodless rite that confers standing, plant and symbolic gift and no animal; 2. the ofo is conferred by the eze ana, which is the licence to officiate; 3. the consecration, in which the senior priest says:

"Ị bụzi oche Agwu. Eziokwu ka ị na-ekwu, n'agbanyeghị na ọ ga-ata gị ụta. Ọbara adịghị n'aka gị; ụgha

adịghị n'ire gị."

You are now the seat of Agwu. Truth you speak, even if it brings bitterness. No blood stains your

hands; no falsehood stains your tongue.

And the words are apt in a way they were not before: "no blood stains your hands" is the scripture's own line, and in Odiana it is literally true of every priest.

The titled body — Nze na Ozo

The lay order, taken and not given. Ozo is not hereditary; it is achieved and paid for, and open to men who meet the requirements.

The rungs below Ozo are three — Ima Mmau at about nine; Ichi with its six stages; and Nli Nwammadu, the novitiate, gated on marriage. Ozo itself is a nine-stage sequence, ending in twenty-one days' seclusion and the Ebo confession and entry in the register.

And the obligations are the substance of the rank — the annual public confession, the taboos of the rank, and the four roles the title confers: ritual, social, political and economic. The titled body's mandate is in one sentence: to admit, to enforce correct payment and ritual, to run the market under the ofo staff, to distribute dividends, and to police the rules.

And the women's ladder runs beside it — inyom → Umokpu → ilimmadunato → Nne Mmau — with its own titles and its own standing. Odiana keeps the parallel ladder (constitution.md §2).

10 · Afa — and what happens when a reading fails

The sixteen signs are read as pairs, right to left. Four beads to a chaplet give sixteen dispositions; two chaplets thrown together give 256, read at the intersection; all four closed is akwu, all four open is obi. Interpretation depends on Agwu — and the doctrine is "Agwu reveals through afa", not that afa is Agwu.

And a reading is falsifiable:

1. each sign carries a dominant theme; 2. the diviner checks whether the themes thrown match the theme of the question asked; 3. a mismatch means Agwu is lying — cured by a horn-blast and a praise-song; 4. if the mismatch persists, the diviner abandons the session and the client returns another day.

"If the afa throws continue to be out of tune with the client's main theme of enquiry, the predictor

generally abandons his efforts and pleads with his client to come back another day."

The rule for Odiana's diviners is therefore: a reading that does not answer the question is not a reading, and the diviner says so. No session is stretched to fit. And the tradition's own prohibition stands — a diviner must not talk openly about what he reads.

11 · The year

The Nzemabua announces the year in Igu Aro, and no Ndose sets its own calendar.

The week is four days — Eke, Orie, Afo, Nkwo — and the year counts thirteen moons. The tradition computes the festival dates from lunations.

And the year is gendered: the offering to men's chi and the offering to women's chi are separate entries in the tradition's own ritual calendar, and Odiana keeps both, each led by its own order.

| festival | is | |---|---| | the new yam | the first fruits — and the tradition's own reduction of a blood sacrifice to a bloodless act, which is the strongest warrant in this liturgy | | the first fruits of any harvest | the same form, at the Ndose | | the water rite | for Idemili: white dress, no kneeling and no bowing, clay vessels, aromatic leaves, and "nothing used pollutes land or water" | | the ancestors' day | at the new moon: the elder cracks kola at the ancestral altar and calls four names — his father, his grandfather, his great-grandfather, and the unknown first planter of the lineage. The ancestors are honoured with nothing killed | | Igu Aro | the announcement of the year, and the day the ground is renewed |

And the assembly decides: major matters are settled under the sacred tree by forty-nine elders, seven times seven, and "the minority, even if wrong, must be heard for three days; for truth often comes from the quietest voice."

The blood ruling, in one place

(The ruling is canon.md A11, and it is the same in every document of this religion.)

An animal is killed at every festival of Odiana and at every serious rite of it. The announcing of the year, the cleansing of a great abomination, the taking of a title, the consecration of a Dibia, the setting of a boundary, the burial of a head, the making of peace, and the opening of a war. The animal is killed in the open, and its blood is spilled upon open ground, away from every holy thing.

And no blood is brought to a shrine, or to an altar, or to a sacred object, or to a tree that is held sacred. Nothing holy in this religion is ever touched with blood. The altar keeps the kola, and the nzu, and the wine, and the water. This is a modernisation of Odinana and it is iwu — made, and published, and dated — and it is not a custom recovered from the ancestors.

What remains bloodless, and stays bloodless:

  • the offering to Chukwu — the tradition's own offering was kola, white chalk and libation, and it is kept;
  • the household shrine — the household oblation is kola, nzu, mmanya and water;
  • the temple altar — no blood is brought to it, ever;
  • the consecration of objects — no shrine, Ofo, Ikenga or medicine is made with blood (canon.md A6);
  • a reading of afa — the reading is free: nothing is charged for it, and the offering is not a fee.

And the one blood that is never shed in this religion, in any rite and for any purpose, is human blood. Where the old practice used a human being, this religion uses the fowl — for it is the fowl that is used in performing sacrifice, and not a human being.
